item.content:encoded:
If spikebrennan approves, some suggested test logs:

Six identical amphibious drones carried to the island by boat, one from each of the six known access points. Drones roped together into a single jury-rigged unit and programmed to travel out of the SCP's known range and return. Combined drones exit as normal from Finland location. Stocktake confirms rope was brought to SCP-908 from Finnish access point.

Previous test is repeated with six new drones and six identical lengths of rope, one of each brought in via each point of access. Combined drones exit SCP's known range and all remote contact is lost. After 24 minutes, contact is re-established via satellite link. The drones have reappeared at [EXPUNGED], a location not previously known to be related to SCP-908 phenomena. GIS analysis suggests the point of emergence is the point on earth that is the shortest distance from all six SCP-908 access points.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
So… what happens if you get two boats (presumably remote-controlled or automated) to approach the island from exactly the same angle at the same speed? In theory they would appear in the island's shared space simultaneously… Very curious as to what the result would be… Boom? Two boats merged together? Or something unexpected?

Ooooh, another idea… Teams from the six known access points bring a boat in pieces and assemble it on the island. Where does the intact boat end up when it leaves? Presuming that your leaving point is dictated by your entry point, then a combined mass from two points (e.g. a man on a boat, or a man in a sea monster's tummy) goes to whatever access point the majority of that mass came from. If it's fairly evenly split between multiple access points… what then?

This also applies to catching a sea monster. It could only be brought into our world if the cage/boat/whatever used to transport it has a higher mass than the creature inside it. Would this mean that it would also need to bring its own water?

Woah… If a vessel could carry greater than its own weight in SCP-908's local water (easy for a lightweight inflatable) then where would it end up when it leaves..?

Really fascinated by the implications of this one.

item.content:encoded: Added oracle bone script, but with an indication that someone carved it recently. How do you like dem apples? Oh, and your heading when you leave the islet is irrelevant. If you arrive at the islet from location X, when you leave (generally speaking, and subject to some not-fully-understood qualifications as indicated in the test log), you return to location X regardless of your vector of approach to the islet or your vector of departure from the islet. Fr'instance, if you arrived at the islet from Duluth, Minnesota (by traveling more or less eastward), then when you leave the island, if you keep going eastward you will eventually hit the Upper Peninsula just as if you had visited a non-anomalous rock during the journey.

Sidestepped. I added:
The islet is frequently surrounded by a mist or fog which interferes with visibility. Under typical daytime conditions, a visitor to the islet is unable to see an object, such as a boat, that is more than 100 meters from the islet. Lighting conditions, atmospheric and water temperatures, and the salinity of the surrounding water remain relatively constant regardless of the time of day or year that the islet is visited, or the point of origin from which it is approached.
